EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
Hot Wheels Unboxing: 10 Special Ferraris I Bought for November of 2026
142 photos
Photo: autoevolution
I wish every one of my diecast unboxing stories had a special topic. It’s easier said than done, even though I’m currently doing three of them each month. It’s particularly complicated when I decide to go for a special group of vehicles, like I have today.
There’s this one story I’ve been putting off for months now. As I know how complicated things can feel like in the hobby in 2026, I figured I’d do a comparison between Hot Wheels collectibles and cars from other brands.
I’ve got Matchbox, Maisto, Mini GT and IXO on my list. And I just wasn’t happy with the Car Culture 2-Pack I had bought for the story, so I upgraded to two Elite 64 models.
These should theoretically be on the same price level as Mini GT and IXO, but they’re more expensive than the Matchbox and Maisto models.
Oh well, it’s not like I could come with a definitive verdict on which brands you should focus on next in just one unboxing story. And anyway, you’re all free to choose the tiny cars that you genuinely love, regardless of my take on the topic.
Photo: autoevolution I’m just here to shine some light on the topic, hoping it will help you avoid spending too much in the wrong direction. I’ve been thinking about a Ferrari -only unboxing ever since Mattel announced the license renewal.
I’ve included some of the modern era castings in my stories since, but deep down I knew I wanted a closer look at what happened before 2015.
And I seized the opportunity the moment I spotted it, even though I paid circa $150 for just 10 Hot Wheels to get here. It might not seem like a lot if you’re an avid RLC collector.
However, from my perspective, it’s the same budget I’d spend on a complete Mainline case, or a Premium set of 10 cars plus something extra. And there’s only one vehicle on today’s list that has Real Riders wheels.
Ferrari F40 Photo: autoevolution I can tell you that this was easily the most expensive item here, but I knew I couldn’t let it go. After all, it’s also the only car here to feature an opening part.
It’s the kind of feature only a few Hot Wheels Ferraris have ever had. In the modern era, it only happened for the 1969 Ferrari 312 P and the F40, both of which were only available as Red Line Club models.
I’ve seen some people listing the latter for as much as $600 on eBay, which is absolutely ridiculous considering my dealer is selling a KKK 1:12th-scale F40 for less than $200.
To each their own I guess. The reason this F40 is so special is that it’s Larry Wood’s creation from the late ‘80s.
Photo: autoevolution It debuted in the 1989 Speed Fleet series and it was available all the way until its 2014 5-Pack release. I believe that was the only iteration that did not have a ZAMAC base, or an opening hood.
The one I have here was part of the Mainline series in the year 2000, and I absolutely love the card art from that period.
As for the car itself, it doesn’t look nearly as accurate as Shawn Moghadam modern Competizione casting. There’s no mechanism to keep the hood open, and it’s seriously loose and not a perfect fit like you’d get with Pop Race items these days.
I realize we’re into a different price league already, but that’s just how far the hobby has gone. Still, the nostalgia element balances things off, and this is certainly one of my collection’s highlights right now.
Ferrari 250 Photo: autoevolution The Ferrari 250 is the second of three Larry Wood -designed castings on today’s list, and it’s also the car with the second longest “career” here.
It was on the market for 18 years, starting with the 1991 Mainline series. Mattel was still using Black Wall wheels at the time, something that just wouldn’t work today.
Fast forward to 1995, its 5-pack iteration showed up with 7-Spoke wheels and a green paint job: I’d almost say it was identical to the car I have here.
It 1996 it showed up as a Treasure Hunt release, complete with Deep Dish Real Riders: I spotted one listed for $29 on eBay but it could be too good to be true.
Photo: autoevolution The one I found is #452 dating back to the 1996 Mainline series. You’ll notice the card art is a bit older by comparison and I enjoy seeing the back too: it’s a real time machine!
I don’t own any of the Speed Fleet, Speed Demons or Action Command collectibles there, but I’m certainly familiar with the Sharkcruiser as I have discussed it before.
This Metalflake Dark Green finish reminds me of Dave Weise’s ‘97 Corvette , but I couldn’t find it for a head-to-head comparison. In 1996, Mattel used three wheel variations on this car.
While I don’t think these 7-spokes are the best choice available, they’re still a clear sign that we’re dealing with an old collectible. You’ll find several iterations of the 250 with either Real Riders or Co-Molded wheels on the market, and it all came to an end in 2009 when it was reduced to a simple Mystery Car.
Ferrari F355 Photo: autoevolution The team in El Segundo has already “revived” the F40 for the modern era of Hot Wheels Ferraris, and you can already hunt for the 250 GTO if that’s what you like.
So, how about the F355? Ronald Wong designed the new one for next year’s Ferrari 80th Anniversary 5-Pack , and it’s quite stunning with that Nero Daytona (black) finish and those Star 5-Spoke wheels.
It will take a while before I can park it next to Larry Wood’s old design, though. This model debuted in the 1995 Model Series.
Coolio’s Gangsta's Paradise was the top hit on Billboard’s list that year, Bill Clinton was serving his first term as the President of the United States of America and Blizzard Entertainment had released Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness (one of my all-time favorite video games!).
Photo: autoevolution Now that I’ve hopefully transported you back to the mid ‘90s, imagine what owning a Ferrari F355 must have been like. My uncle had a Kadett at the time, and it felt like a rocket ship with 81 horsepower on tap, while the F355 was packing 375 hp from its 3.5 liter V8.
I just had a quick look at BaT’s auction results, and prices seem to vary between $90,000 to $355,355 for one of these cars. That means I’ll have to settle for the 1/64th-scale version for now. At least I’m the happy owner of one of the first iterations to ever come out of the factory.
I’d give up the 5-Dot wheels for a set of Saw-blade rims any day of the week. You can also opt for three other designs in that department, as they were all available that same year.
While the 355 got a Treasure Hunt release in 1996, its final version is likely still the most desired one as it was part of the Ferrari Racer series and had CM6 rims to show off. It could cost around $100 if you’re willing to go that far.
Ferrari F50 Spider Photo: autoevolution That was the last of the yellow Ferraris for today’s story. There’s no Nero Daytona in here today, so you’ll have to settle for two more grey ones and five cars in the iconic red finish.
At least the 250 was special in green, right? I know asking 100 people what their ultimate dream car is could render 100 different answers.
I’m sure some of them will include the McLaren F1, the Lamborghini Diablo and the Ferrari F40. But I’ve been stuck thinking about the F50 ever since I was six or seven years old and my mom bought me a Bburago version of the car.
Being able to race it in Need for Speed II around the same period further fueled that fire, and I almost fainted when I saw one in the real world back in 2015. If I could only ever drive one Ferrari in my life, this would be the one.
Photo: autoevolution And there’s no better way to enjoy that F1-derived V12 in the back than by having the top down. Michael Kollins designed both this Spider version and the Challenge model, and you could say the latter was a bit more successful having been available between 1999 and 2013.
The Spider debuted in the 1996 First Editions series alongside the 1996 Mustang GT which I just recently unboxed. It’s always exciting to have the first version of a certain Hot Wheels item in your collection, and I don’t think I can ever let it go.
My dealer also had the Metalflake Purple version of the car (last one to ever come out of the factory), but I just had to choose this red car even though it cost twice as much.
You can find it in yellow too and I truly hope that’s what Mattel will use for Ronald Wong’s casting next. The old car definitely feels outdated when parked next to the modern era casting, which doesn’t make it any less exciting.
Ferrari Testarossa Photo: autoevolution The Ferrari F40 is the heaviest collectible on today’s list: at 56 grams it’s in the Top100 out of a total of almost 400 Hot Wheels I’ve unboxed since last year.
The Ferrari Testarossa isn’t that far behind, as it proves Mattel’s products in the ‘90s had more metal in them than they do today (even when comparing old Mainline to new Premium cars).
Of course this isn’t a definitive verdict, and I guess some people might not even care about the way these items “perform” on the scales.
I enjoying documenting the observation, though. At first, I thought the Testarossa I had just bought was Larry Wood’s design from the late ‘80s. I realized something was off after not being able to identify any variation of it with the 5-Dot wheels.
Photo: autoevolution Mattel retired the design in 1998, making way for the F512M/Testarossa that Michael Kollins worked on (he designed nine Ferraris during his tenure, and we’ve got five of them here today). The Metalflake Silver version was the First Edition release in 1998, rolling on either 5DOT or 5-Spoke rims.
They both had a metal base though, and I wish I could get a closer look at the 1999 Treasure Hunt iteration with the PC5 wheels.
Given how window shopping is completely free, I’d also probably skip the Ferrari Racer Testarossa and go straight for the 2013 Retro Entertainment: Miami Vice that also closed the chapter for the design.
I used a small flashlight when taking a photo of the rear section of the new and old cars so you can see the difference 30+ years have made. I’m almost certain collectors would keep buying modern variations of the ‘90s casting as it’s still fairly impressive today.
Ferrari 360 Modena Photo: autoevolution Nissan reportedly built just under 12,000 units of the Skyline GT-R (R34), while most people will tell you Ferrari probably only made less than 9,000 360 Modenas.
So, if you ignore the Spider version of the Italian sports car, it’s quite a bit rarer than “Godzilla”. Now, a quick look at the used market: The cheapest GT-R on BaT traded hands for $105,000 this year, while the most expensive one went for $444,444.
Meanwhile, someone was lucky enough to get a Modena for $70,666, while the coolest one sold for $325,000. Let’s not talk about Challenge Stradale options though. What I’m trying to say here is this.
If you could only afford one car, you’d have to be out of your damn mind to pick the GT-R instead of the 360 Modena. I don’t even care about lap times, running costs, or tuning possibilities, these machines are in different leagues.
Photo: autoevolution And the fun part is that you can still find a way to buy the Ferrari, even if you’re not a millionaire. Yes, I am worried about the maintenance at this point, but it’s not something you have to deal with in the 1/64th-scale Universe.
Also, can you believe this casting is almost 30 years old at this point? I’d be shocked if Mattel doesn’t come up with a modern era version of it in 2027 or 2028 the latest.
But I can also survive on collecting more variations of the design Michael Kollins worked on. Mine is another First Editions release, and I’m happy to report that it has a metal base. In 2001 it showed up in black with PR5 wheels, and you’ll find the same design on a few more iterations.
I know some collectors will be eager to look for the four Ferrari Racer models, but those can easily cost over $50 a pop. The Auto Affinity: Got Speed version will only be half as expensive and it’s running on genuine Real Riders rims!
Ferrari F355 Challenge Photo: autoevolution You could say 1999 was a good year for Hot Wheels Ferrari enthusiasts. Not only did we get the 360 Modena, but also the F355 Challenge back then.
I’m unsure why the latter isn’t a “First Editions” release though. This thing had a metal base, which is why it weighs 47 grams, on par with the newer basic GMC Motorhome and the premium McLaren Speedtail I unboxed recently.
Buying a real world F355 Challenge might be complicated, considering only 108 were reportedly built. What Michael Kollins achieved here is seriously impressive, and it makes Larry Wood’s old F355 look seriously outdated by comparison.
While I’d normally be annoyed by the gray finish, the stripes running down the middle and the racing decals are a big plus.
Photo: autoevolution We’ve got Beta Tools, Magneti Marelli and Pirelli to name a few, and then there’s the spoiler. It just needs detailed tail lights and Real Riders wheels at this point.
Mattel switched to yellow for the next two years and four variations, and a red F355 Challenge didn’t show up until 2003.
For 2007, 2008 and 2009 it advanced to the Ferrari Racer series and even I have to admit that the black one was amazing with orange wheels on.
This casting has just as long of a lifespan as the 360 Modena and the 333 SP I’m about to dive into next.
Ferrari 333 SP Photo: autoevolution If you were looking for the fastest car on today’s list, you’ve just found it. It’s obviously not the only one here with a V12 engine inside but it’s a racing machine first and foremost and it weighs less than a first-generation Mazda MX-5 (under 2,000 lbs/907 kg!).
Ferrari only made 40 of them (with Dallara and Michelotto onboard the project as well). I think you could have bought one for less than $1 million back in 2011, and it won’t be remotely as easy to do so today.
I’ve seen one racing down the main straight at Mugello about a decade ago, and it’s probably the closest I’ve gotten to a ‘90s F1 machine engaged in WOT mode.
You have to hear it to believe it! The 333 SP was the first Hot Wheels Ferrari Mark Jones worked on, and it wouldn’t be his last. His 156 is on my Must Have list for the near future, and the same goes for his Enzo and 250 LM.
Photo: autoevolution Honestly, it’s almost surreal for me to have the first-ever release of the 333 SP in my collection, even though I’m not completely happy with the Wire Spoke wheels.
The PR5s are slightly better, and I wish the team would have used something similar on the Hall of Fame: Milestone Moments too.
The blue livery on the 2002 Ferrari 5-Pack variation is just as enticing, and I’m not even upset this is one of the lightest items on my list for today. I just wish I still had some of the other ‘90s IMSA Racers at home for the photo shoot: both the Cadillac LMP and Riley & Scott MK III are long gone.
Now I suddenly have the urge to go back to the original Assetto Corsa for a lap in the Porsche 917/30.
Ferrari 550 Maranello Photo: autoevolution I don’t know about you, but I’m not a fan of Porsches or Ferraris that have a front-mounted engine. Some of them can still be incredibly fast, but I feel a big part of the supercar experience is gone once you choose that layout.
You’ll notice that the 550 Maranello is only one of two such machines on this list, and we could give the 250 a pass considering how old and rare it is.
The 550 debuted back in 1996, and my first contact with it happened in circa 2002 with Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit 2.
That game featured the rarer, Barchetta Pininfarina version, though, and I can’t say it had any effect on me as I was happier in either the 360 Spider or the F50.
Photo: autoevolution I might just start a special “First Editions” display at home when I’ll have enough space to do so, as this 550 Maranello was part of that series in the year 2000.
I’ve see photos of an alternate release for this debut iteration which had silver headlights and I’m glad to have the regular version instead.
Production ended in 2013 with a Speed Machines variation that didn’t even have the Co-Molded wheels on anymore.
You’ll have to search for the 2011 550 Maranello to enjoy those, or the 2009 Ferrari Racer if you don’t mind paying $40 to $100 for one. You won’t find any Real Riders rims here, and the 575 GTC didn’t get them either.
Ferrari Enzo Photo: autoevolution I missed the pre-order window on this year’s Boulevard Mix 4, and I knew that meant I would never be able to find the Ferrari Enzo for its regular retail price.
When someone in our local collector’s group listed it for $16, I immediately ordered two as I was sure my buddy Omar would want it as well.
It was ultimately a bit cheaper than the F50, which I paid about $19 for. At least I secured a pre-order for the F40, which means chasing after the 288 GTO is the next logical step to get all the Big 5s under the same roof.
The LaFerrari is the one I’m least excited about. There’s even less nostalgia involved with the F80, which is bound to show up within the next two to three years.
Photo: autoevolution Anyway, Ronald Wong did an amazing job with the Enzo, and this thing definitely sets a new standard for future Boulevard/Car Culture collectibles.
A comparison with Tomica’s take on the car might have been interesting if it didn’t have those hideous wheels on.
I haven’t heard any news about a new variation for 2027, but I’m keeping my fingers crossed for a Giallo Modena finish. How long before we get a Ferrari-exclusive set?
The Big 5 makes the most sense, and it could easily become one the most hyped mixes in Hot Wheels history when it happens. I say “when” because I’m certain there’s no need to use “if” here. I’ll be back with my next unboxing story soon!
